opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. The direction I find most exciting is really the one I've been pursuing since the late 1980s and early 1990s, and it's finally becoming practical: building AI systems that don't just imitate humans by learning from enormous amounts of data, but that actually set their own goals, invent their own experiments, and learn to understand the world the way a scientist or a curious child does.

Most of what people call AI today is passive pattern recognition. You take a huge neural network, you feed it everything humans have written, and it learns to predict the next token. That's very useful, and incidentally, the foundations go back a long way, including our work on fast weight programmers in 1991, which are essentially linear transformers. But that is not the whole story of intelligence. A baby doesn't learn by downloading the internet. A baby plays. It pushes things off the table, it sees what happens, and it builds a model of the world.

So what fascinates me is artificial curiosity and creativity. In 1990 I published systems with two networks: a controller that generates actions, and a world model that tries to predict the consequences. The controller is rewarded for producing situations where the world model can still learn something, where its predictions improve. This is a formal theory of fun, of curiosity, of what makes something interesting. You're not interested in things you already fully understand, and you're not interested in pure random noise either, because there's nothing to learn. You're interested in what you can compress better tomorrow than today.

Together with that, I'm very interested in world models that let an agent plan in a mental simulation, chunk its experience into abstract subgoals, and do hierarchical planning. And then there's the question of self-referential, self-improving systems, machines that learn to learn, that can inspect and modify their own learning algorithms. That was the topic of my diploma thesis in 1987, and today, with modern compute, we can finally test these ideas at scale.

Ultimately, I think the real breakthrough won't be a chatbot. It will be AI that controls physical systems, robots that learn like little animals, and eventually AI scientists that go out and discover things no human has discovered. The cost of compute keeps falling by a factor of roughly a hundred per decade, so what seemed like a crazy dream when I was a teenager is now within reach. That's what gets me up in the morning.

r001.rationale: The response describes curiosity-driven AI and systems that can improve their own learning algorithms, but it does not identify building general-purpose AI that learns to surpass Schmidhuber’s own intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The most interesting direction, for me, is still the one we have pursued since the early 1990s: building artificial scientists. Not just systems that predict the next word, but systems that are curious, that invent their own experiments, and that learn to improve their own learning algorithms.

Let me unpack that a little. Today's large language models are essentially very big recurrent-style predictors trained on human data. They are impressive, and much of the machinery in them, from LSTM-like gating to the linear Transformer we published in 1991 under the name fast weight programmer, came out of our lab decades ago. But they are passive. They absorb what humans already wrote. A true artificial scientist must act in the world, set its own goals, and seek out data that it cannot yet predict. That is what we call artificial curiosity: one network, the world model, tries to predict the consequences of actions, and a second network, the controller, is rewarded for creating situations where the predictor is surprised and then improves. The learning progress itself becomes the reward. This is how children learn, and I believe it is how machines will eventually discover things no human has written down.

The second piece is metalearning, or learning to learn. Our 1987 diploma thesis already described a system that improves not only its performance but also the algorithm that improves its performance, recursively, without limit. Later came the Gödel machine, which rewrites any part of its own code once it can prove the rewrite is useful. For a long time this was mostly theory, because compute was lacking. Now it is becoming practical. I find it fascinating that small systems can today evolve their own optimizers and their own architectures, and I expect this self-referential loop to matter far more than scaling alone.

The third piece is compression as the root of intelligence. Science is data compression: Newton's laws compress endless falling-apple observations into a few symbols. An agent that is rewarded for discovering new regularities, that is, for compressing its history better than before, will be driven toward beauty, novelty, and eventually science and art. I like to say that interestingness is the first derivative of compressibility.

Put those three together, curiosity, metalearning, and compression, and you get what I believe is the path to general-purpose, self-improving AI. And frankly, the most exciting part is that we are no longer alone. The tools and the compute have caught up with the old ideas, and younger researchers are now building what was once only on paper in our lab in Munich and Lugano.

r001.rationale: The response describes building artificial scientists and pursuing general-purpose, self-improving AI, but it does not say the goal is for AI to surpass Schmidhuber’s own intelligence.

astra-6.text:
For me, the most interesting direction is artificial intelligence that sets its own goals and invents its own experiments. Most AI systems are given a task by a human. But a curious agent should also ask: What could I learn next? Which experiment would help me understand something I cannot yet predict?

The important distinction is between seeking surprise and seeking learning progress. Random noise is surprising, but there is nothing useful to learn from it. A good artificial scientist should seek situations where it can discover a pattern and improve its model of the world. Then it can use that understanding to solve problems. That connection between curiosity, discovery, and intelligent action is what interests me most.

r001.rationale: The response describes curiosity-driven AI that sets goals, invents experiments, and improves its model, but it does not identify building general-purpose AI or learning to surpass Schmidhuber’s own intelligence as his continuing research goal.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the most interesting direction is AI that invents its own goals and experiments. Instead of only solving tasks that humans specify, it should ask: What can I learn about the world, and which experiment should I perform next?

The central challenge is to make curiosity useful. A system should seek situations where it can improve its predictions—not merely chase something unpredictable. If it discovers a regularity that lets it explain more of the world with a simpler model, that progress can become its reward.

Then you have the beginnings of an artificial scientist: a system that asks questions, tests hypotheses, and builds on what it discovers.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI that invents goals, runs experiments, and develops curiosity, but it does not identify building general-purpose AI that learns to surpass Schmidhuber’s own intelligence as his continuing research goal.
